content: Aniline, also known as phenylamine or aminobenzene, is an organic compound with the chemical formula C6H5NH2. It is the simplest aromatic amine and serves as a precursor for the synthesis of more complex chemicals. Its primary industrial application is in the production of polyurethane. Aniline has a distinct, unpleasant odor reminiscent of rotten fish and a burning, acrid taste. It is highly toxic and ignites easily, producing a smoky flame when burned. Structurally, aniline consists of a phenyl group (C6H5-) attached to an amino group (-NH2). Industrially, aniline is synthesized from benzene in a two-step process. First, benzene undergoes nitration with a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and sulfuric acid at 50–60°C, producing nitrobenzene. This nitrobenzene is then subjected to hydrogenation in the presence of a nickel catalyst at approximately 600°C, yielding aniline. Numerous derivatives of aniline can be synthesized using similar methods. Commercially, three main types of aniline are recognized: aniline oil for blue, which is pure aniline; aniline oil for red, a mixture of aniline with orthoand para-toluidines; and aniline oil for safranine, which contains aniline and ortho-toluidine and is derived from the distillation of fuchsine. Aniline is a colorless liquid that gradually oxidizes when exposed to air, resulting in a red-brown discoloration in aged samples. Its oxidation reactions have been extensively studied. In alkaline solutions, aniline oxidizes to form azobenzene, while arsenic acid produces violaniline, a violet-colored compound. Chromic acid converts aniline into quinone, and chlorates in the presence of metallic salts, particularly vanadium, yield aniline black. Potassium permanganate oxidizes aniline to nitrobenzene in neutral solutions, to azobenzene, ammonia, and oxalic acid in alkaline solutions, and to aniline black in acidic solutions. Hypochlorous acid reacts with aniline to produce 4-aminophenol and para-amino diphenylamine. Aniline is a weak base, as is typical of aromatic amines, which are less basic than aliphatic amines. When reacted with strong acids, aniline forms the anilinium ion (C6H5-NH3+), and its sulfate salt crystallizes into white plates. Despite its weak basicity, aniline can precipitate salts of zinc, aluminum, and iron, and it can release ammonia from ammonium salts upon heating. Aniline undergoes acylation reactions with carboxylic acids or, more readily, with acyl chlorides such as acetyl chloride, forming amides. These amides are sometimes referred to as anilides. For example, acetanilide (CH3-CO-NH-C6H5) is formed from the reaction of aniline with acetic acid or acetyl chloride. Acetanilide, also known as Antifebrin, was historically used as a medication. Aniline reacts with alkyl iodides to form secondary and tertiary amines. Monomethyl aniline and dimethyl aniline are important compounds in the dye industry. These are synthesized by heating aniline, aniline hydrochloride, and methanol in an autoclave at 220°C. Monomethyl aniline has a boiling point of 193–195°C, while dimethyl aniline boils at 192°C. When boiled with carbon disulfide, aniline forms sulfocarbanilide (diphenyl thiourea), which can be further decomposed into phenyl isothiocyanate and triphenyl guanidine. Aniline derivatives, like phenols, are highly reactive to electrophilic substitution. For instance, sulfonation of aniline produces sulfanilic acid, which can be converted into sulfanilamide, a compound historically used as an antibacterial agent. Sulfanilic acid is synthesized by reacting aniline with sulfuric acid at 180°C. Aniline and its derivatives react with nitrous acid to form diazonium salts, which are intermediates in the Sandmeyer reactions. These reactions allow the conversion of the -NH2 group in aniline to other functional groups such as -OH, -CN, or halides. Historically, aniline gained commercial importance due to its role in the production of dyes. The discovery of mauveine, the first synthetic dye, by William Henry Perkin in 1856, marked the beginning of the synthetic dye industry. Aniline was initially expensive but became more accessible through industrial-scale production methods. Aniline-based dyes, such as fuchsine, safranine, and indulines, revolutionized the dyeing industry. Beyond dyes, aniline is a precursor for the synthesis of various drugs, including paracetamol (acetaminophen). It is also used in histological staining, such as the Nissl stain for neural RNA. Currently, the largest market for aniline is in the production of methylene diphenyl diisocyanate (MDI), which accounts for approximately 85% of its use. Other applications include rubber processing chemicals (9%), herbicides (2%), and dyes and pigments (2%). Aniline was first isolated in 1826 by Otto Unverdorben during the destructive distillation of indigo. Friedrich Runge later identified a substance in coal tar that produced a blue color when treated with chloride of lime, naming it kyanol or cyanol. In 1841, C.J. Fritzsche obtained aniline by treating indigo with caustic potash, naming it after the indigo plant Indigofera anil. Around the same time, N.N. Zinin synthesized aniline by reducing nitrobenzene. August Wilhelm von Hofmann later confirmed that these substances were identical, establishing the compound as aniline or phenylamine. The first industrial use of aniline was in the production of mauveine, discovered by Perkin in 1856. The synthetic dye industry rapidly expanded with the discovery of additional aniline-based dyes in the late 19th century. Aniline is toxic and poses significant health risks through inhalation, skin absorption, or ingestion. Aniline was implicated in the toxic oil syndrome outbreak in Spain in 1981, which caused widespread illness and fatalities. While some authorities classify aniline as a potential carcinogen, the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) places it in Group 3, indicating that its carcinogenicity to humans is not classifiable due to limited and conflicting evidence.
